segments.speaker: greg
segments.transcript:
My first private contract was for a bakery.

Not a monster.

Not a bridge.

Not a dead station.

Bread.

The bakery was downstairs from our apartment.

I had lived over it for years.

I knew when the morning batch started because the floor warmed under the bed.

I knew when the youngest baker was late because the ovens came up unevenly.

I knew when they burned rye because Nessa opened every window and complained as though smoke had entered the apartment deliberately.

segments.speaker: greg
segments.transcript:
I did not know the owner's name until she knocked on our door with money in her hand.

That was embarrassing.

“Greg?”

“Yes.”

She was small, maybe fifty, flour on one sleeve.

“You work the Line.”

“Yes.”

“Can you look at my oven feed?”

“Call district service.”

“I did.”

“What did they say?”

“Fourteen days.”

“That sounds about right.”

She held up three silver.

“Can you look today?”

I looked at the coins.

Then at her.

“Is this a bribe?”

“No.”

“Good.”

segments.speaker: greg
segments.transcript:
“What is the difference?”

“I don't know yet.”

From behind me, Nessa said, “If she gives you the money before you do the work, it is probably a contract.”

The woman looked past me.

“Nessa.”

“Morning, Mina.”

There it was.

Mina.

Apparently Nessa knew the person who had been baking under our feet for six years.

I turned.

“You know her?”

Nessa stared at me.

“She gave us the table.”

I looked at Mina.

Mina looked at me.

“The table came with the rooms,” I said.

segments.speaker: greg
segments.transcript:
“No,” Mina said. “It didn't.”

Nessa started laughing.

I learned several things that morning.

Mina Cor owned the bakery and the building.

Our table had belonged to her brother.

Private Line work required a Guild notice if I touched anything past the building shutoff.

And I had spent years assigning emotional significance to a piece of furniture without knowing where it came from.

That last one was less relevant to the contract.

Probably.

segments.speaker: greg
segments.transcript:
The Guild notice took an hour.

SITE.

CLIENT.

SCOPE.

RANK OR TRADE AUTHORITY.

FEE.

I stared at the last line.

The clerk said, “Yes, you have to write what you're charging.”

“Why?”

“So when you claim you were helping a friend after something explodes, we can see whether the friend paid you.”

“That happens?”

“Often enough to make the line.”

Institutions again.

Scars with boxes.

I wrote three silver.

The clerk looked at it.

“For inspection and repair?”

segments.speaker: greg
segments.transcript:
“I don't know if it needs repair.”

“So inspection.”

“Yes.”

“Three is low.”

“I live upstairs.”

“That is not a pricing method.”

“It is today.”

She stamped it.

The bakery lost oven pressure every morning between fifth and sixth bell.

Only then.

District pressure held steady.

Building pressure did not.

Mina had replaced the gauge twice.

The ovens were fine. Three bakers explained that to me at once with their arms folded.

I checked the shutoff.

Fine.

segments.speaker: greg
segments.transcript:
Branch valve.

Fine.

Heat exchanger.

Dirty, but fine.

Then I did what I had started doing too often.

I looked for the interesting answer.

Hidden connection.

Legacy sleeve.

Pressure migrating through old construction.

I was halfway under a floor hatch when Lorn walked in carrying breakfast.

He looked down at my legs.

“What are you doing?”

“Working.”

“Dera said you had the day off.”

“I do.”

He looked around the bakery.

Then at Mina.

Then back at me.

segments.speaker: greg
segments.transcript:
“Working.”

“Privately.”

He bit into a roll.

“You getting paid?”

“Yes.”

“How much?”

“None of your business.”

Mina said, “Three silver.”

Traitor.

Lorn almost choked.

“Three?”

“What?”

“For a building-side pressure fault?”

“Yes.”

“You are terrible at money.”

“I have a ledger.”

“That makes it worse.”

I climbed out from under the floor.

“What do you think?” I asked.

“Hot-water draw.”

“You have been here thirty seconds.”

“I've bought bread here nine years.”

segments.speaker: greg
segments.transcript:
He pointed toward the back wall.

“Fifth bell. They wash yesterday's trays.”

One of the bakers looked over.

“Yes.”

Lorn pointed at the exchanger.

“Same manifold?”

Mina nodded.

I looked at the oven branch.

Then the hot-water branch.

Same manifold.

Undersized balancing valve.

No buried civilization required.

We ran the wash draw.

Oven pressure dropped.

There it was.

Simple after somebody noticed the building had people in it.

I had inspected metal.

segments.speaker: greg
segments.transcript:
Lorn had inspected the morning.

“Inspector,” he said.

“Fuck you.”

We could have replaced the valve.

Mina did not want to pay for that.

So we changed the wash sequence and fitted a cheap restrictor on the hot-water branch. Lorn did most of the fitting while I watched the gauges.

Three silver became four because Mina insisted he should be paid.

I gave him one.

He stared at the coin.

“That's too much.”

“You said three was too little.”

“For you.”
